title: Being brought before a court in time
summary: If you are arrested, the police must bring you before a court within a reasonable time - broadly one day where a court is nearby, or two days otherwise.
body_plain: The Constitution requires that anyone who is arrested and detained be brought before a court within a reasonable time. It explains 'reasonable time' as, in general, one day where there is a court within about forty kilometres, and two days (or such longer period a court considers reasonable) in other cases. If this does not happen, your continued detention may be unlawful and you may be entitled to release.
rights: You must be brought before a court within a reasonable time (s.35(4)).
'Reasonable time' is broadly one or two days depending on distance to a court (s.35(5)).
Detention beyond the lawful time may entitle you to release.
do_list: Note the exact date and time of your arrest.
Ask when you will be taken to court.
Have your lawyer raise any delay beyond the lawful limit.
dont_list: Do not assume long detention without charge is normal or lawful.
Do not sign anything agreeing to be held indefinitely.
common_situations: You remain at a police station while officers repeatedly postpone taking you to court.
A weekend or public holiday is used as a vague explanation for continued detention.
Your family is told you will be charged but no court, date, or case information is provided.
words_to_use: When and before which court will I be brought?
Please record the exact time of my arrest and my request to be taken before a court.
Allow me to contact my lawyer or a person of my choice about my detention.
if_violated: Keep a detailed timeline of arrest, transfers, interviews, bail requests, and every promised court date.
Ask relatives and witnesses to preserve messages, calls, visitor records, and proof of the place of detention.
Seek urgent legal help to challenge continued detention and obtain the custody records.
